definitions.definition: A mapping between two systems that shows they have the same structure, even if they look different on the surface.
definitions.example: A map of a subway system is isomorphic to the actual subway lines — the connections are the same even though the map is smaller and simplified.

definitions.definition: A law stating that light intensity decreases exponentially as it passes through a material that absorbs some of it.
definitions.example: When you shine a flashlight through a glass of dark soda, the light gets dimmer the deeper it goes — that's the Beer-Lambert Law in action.

definitions.definition: The process where a fee is taken out of every payment as it moves through a financial system, like a toll on a highway.
definitions.example: Every time you use a credit card to buy coffee, the bank takes a small percentage of the money — that's transaction extraction.

definitions.definition: A pattern where something decreases by a fixed percentage over equal steps, getting smaller and smaller but never reaching zero.
definitions.example: A bouncing ball that loses 10% of its height each bounce follows exponential decay — it goes 100 cm, 90 cm, 81 cm, and so on.

definitions.definition: A material that soaks up some of the energy passing through it, like a sponge soaking up water.
definitions.example: A tinted window is an absorptive medium for light — it lets some light through but absorbs the rest as heat.

definitions.definition: The distance a wave or signal travels through a material.
definitions.example: If you shine a laser through a 1-meter tank of water, the path length is 1 meter.

definitions.definition: A number that tells how strongly a material absorbs light or other signals per unit of distance.
definitions.example: Dark sunglasses have a high absorption coefficient for visible light; clear glass has a low one.

definitions.definition: A group or system that sits between two parties in a transaction, taking a cut for its services.
definitions.example: Visa and Mastercard are part of the intermediary layer between you and the store when you pay with a card.

definitions.definition: A fee that a bank charges a store every time a customer uses a credit card, usually a small percentage of the purchase.
definitions.example: When you buy a $10 pizza with a credit card, the store might pay a 30-cent interchange fee to the bank.

definitions.definition: The process where a system loses its order, harmony, or integrity over time, becoming more chaotic or broken.
definitions.example: A well-organized team that starts arguing and missing deadlines is experiencing coherence degradation.

definitions.definition: Describes a system that loses some of the original signal or energy as it passes through, like a fuzzy radio station.
definitions.example: A cheap audio cable is lossy — the music sounds muffled because some signal is lost.

definitions.definition: The idea that when new money is created, the people closest to the source benefit first and most, while others lose value later.
definitions.example: If the government prints new money and gives it to banks first, bankers can spend it before prices rise, but you pay more later.

definitions.definition: The study of what kinds of things actually exist in reality.
definitions.example: Asking whether numbers are real things or just ideas is a question about ontology.

definitions.definition: A set of symbols and rules used to describe something precisely, like a mathematical language.
definitions.example: Using equations like E=mc² is a formalism for describing energy and mass.

definitions.definition: The study of how parts of a system are connected, ignoring exact sizes and shapes.
definitions.example: A donut and a coffee cup have the same topology because they both have one hole — you can squish one into the other without tearing.

definitions.definition: Working or applying in both directions, like a two-way street.
definitions.example: A friendship is bidirectional — both people give and receive support.

definitions.definition: Describes a process where the outcome is completely decided by the starting conditions, with no randomness.
definitions.example: If you drop a rock, it will fall straight down every time — that's deterministic.

definitions.definition: The idea that a scientific claim must be testable and could be proven wrong by evidence.
definitions.example: The claim 'all swans are white' can be falsified by finding one black swan.

definitions.definition: A perfect match in the way two systems are built, even if they are about different things.
definitions.example: A family tree and a company org chart can be structurally isomorphic if both have a boss at the top and branches below.

definitions.definition: A basic rule or starting point that is accepted as true without proof, used to build other ideas.
definitions.example: In geometry, 'a straight line is the shortest distance between two points' is an axiom.

definitions.definition: A principle that some quantity (like energy or matter) stays the same over time, even if it changes form.
definitions.example: When you burn wood, the mass turns into ash and smoke, but the total amount of matter stays the same — that's conservation of mass.

definitions.definition: The idea that the total order or harmony in a system cannot be created or destroyed, only moved or changed in form.
definitions.example: If you clean your messy room, the mess doesn't disappear — it moves to the trash can or the closet.
